title: Capt. Thomas Bullitt's 1773 survey party

bodyMarkdown:
In the summer of 1773, Virginia officer [Thomas Bullitt](/people/#thomas-bullitt) led one of the first surveying parties into the Kentucky country. Born about 1730 in Prince William County, Virginia, he had fought in the French and Indian War—at Fort Necessity with Washington, on Braddock’s expedition, and with distinction at Grant’s defeat near Fort Duquesne in 1758. Washington called his conduct “matter of great admiration.” Henry Bouquet wrote that Grant’s force “would probably have been cut to pieces but for Captain Bullet.” By 1772 the College of William & Mary had certified him as a surveyor of a district on the Ohio.

About thirty-four men set out. Isaac Hite and six others joined them on the Ohio. Among the names in the journals are Hancock Taylor, James Douglas, James Harrod, and the McAfee brothers. The McAfees and their associates split off at Big Bone Lick to survey on their own. Bullitt’s party reached the Falls of the Ohio in July 1773 and ran surveys under claims from the Royal Proclamation of 1763. Governor Dunmore later wrote George Washington that he “knew nothing” of Capt. Bullitt’s surveying and had advised him from Fort Pitt to return at once. The surveys went ahead anyway.

That same summer Bullitt is credited with locating the salt spring on the Salt River later called Bullitt’s Lick, a site of early commercial salt for Kentucky settlements and the Illinois country. Family accounts and Lewis Collins’s history said he also laid off Louisville in 1773. An 1882 history of the Falls cities reviewed the diaries, the 1780 town act, and later testimony and found no reliable 1773 plat. Louisville’s half-acre lots came with the settlers of 1778 and a 1779 survey. What Bullitt’s party did leave was a trail of entries and river knowledge that later claimants used.

The work was illegal in Dunmore’s eyes and dangerous on the ground. Shawnee objections to surveyors on hunting ground south of the Ohio were among the grievances that ran into Lord Dunmore’s War the next year. Bullitt himself went home to Fauquier County. In the Revolution he served as Virginia’s adjutant general and as deputy adjutant general in the Southern Department under Charles Lee. He died at his Fauquier home in February 1778, unmarried, leaving his estate to his brother Cuthbert.

Bullitt County, formed in 1796–97 from Jefferson and Nelson, is named for his nephew Alexander Scott Bullitt, Kentucky’s first lieutenant governor under the 1799 constitution—not for the captain. The lick and a roadside marker still carry Thomas’s name. His 1773 party remains one of the earliest documented surveying expeditions into the land that became Kentucky.

## Kentucky today

Kentucky Historical Marker No. 133 stands about three miles northwest of Shepherdsville at the Bullitt’s Lick site. The Falls of the Ohio, where the 1773 party camped, are preserved today as a state park and National Wildlife Conservation Area across from Louisville. Bullitt’s surveys did not found the city, but they opened the salt and river country that made the county.
Source: [Grokipedia: Thomas Bullitt](https://grokipedia.com/page/Thomas_Bullitt)
